prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its physiological actions and its active peptide form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B041 is the one candidate on which all six of us agree for first place, and the agreement rests on the substance. It has a continuous chain from gut-hormone physiology and proglucagon processing, through identification of the active GLP-1 peptide, to receptor agonists with proven cardiovascular, renal and weight benefit in very large randomized trials. The mechanism is understood, the discovery is original, and the clinical impact is now unmistakable. As a clinician I see how much it has changed the treatment of metabolic disease. A prize built on the basic-science trio of Holst (incretin physiology and secretion), Drucker (GLP-1 biology and translation) and Mojsov (identification of the active peptide) honors the discovery of the principle and fits within the three-person limit. I keep B044 and B023 as the next strongest cases because both created a therapeutic modality whose principle has been confirmed clinically: cytokine blockade in one case and engineered T cells in the other.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Priority for the active peptide is disputed, Habener is outside the credited names, and a trio of basic scientists leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting acylated analogues are what actually reached patients. A prize that honors physiology while the drugs carry the clinical impact could be read as crediting the wrong side of the chain. A Mojsov-versus-Knudsen choice is a judgement about discovery versus development that I cannot settle from the supplied evidence, and the committee may reasonably decide that the priority dispute makes the credit too contentious to resolve fairly.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B041, arguing that Knudsen led the long-acting analogue program (liraglutide, semaglutide) and that Mojsov's contribution to the sequence and activity is contested.
responses.response: I take the point that the drugs, not the peptide chemistry, changed practice, and I do not dismiss Knudsen's role. But a Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine has historically rewarded the discovery of the principle, and the incretin principle was established before any pharmaceutical optimization. Mojsov's identification of the truncated, insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) form is the step that made the hormone a therapeutic candidate. Substituting Knudsen would turn the prize into one for drug development, and the committee would then have to explain why the optimization of the molecule outweighs the identification of the active molecule. I would not call Mojsov's contribution contested enough to exclude her on the supplied evidence, though I accept that the priority record needs checking before a final vote.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (B011) second, as a clean two-person discovery of organelle-to-nucleus signalling, confirmed for more than 25 years, while acknowledging that direct medical translation is limited.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori make the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that the mechanism is solid. My reservation is the one Perlmann notes: the human disease link is still largely correlative and no therapy rests on it. I left B011 out of my own top eight because I weigh the medical dimension of the prize heavily. I would not oppose it as a prize for a basic mechanism, but I do not think it should displace a discovery with demonstrated patient benefit in the preferred slot. It is a credible later or companion candidate rather than a front-runner for me.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks TOR signaling (B005) third with Hall and Schreiber, and treats Sabatini's inclusion as less secure because of professional controversy he recalls but cannot verify.
responses.response: I came to the same position by a different route: Hall's genetic identification of TOR is the decisive step, and I ranked B005 with Hall alone. I would not exclude Sabatini on the basis of an unverified controversy, since the committee should decide on scientific contribution and document anything beyond that. But I disagree with adding Schreiber automatically. His FKBP12-rapamycin work was important chemical biology, and it overlaps with other contributors, including Heitman and Movva. A single-laureate or Hall-centred prize looks cleaner to me than the Hall and Schreiber pair, and the clinical benefit of rapalogs is narrower than the cell-biology impact, so I place B005 below the candidates that reached patients.

responses.point: Svenningsson places the cGAS-STING pathway (B029) third, as a clear mechanistic discovery linking infection, autoimmunity and tumour immunity, with Chen as the decisive biochemical step and Barber as the STING identifier.
responses.response: I ranked B029 sixth, so I sit well below you. The scientific case is strong: Chen's cGAS and cGAMP work is a real discovery of a second messenger, and the pathway matters for interferonopathies and lupus, which I know from my own field. But the therapeutic validation you describe as pending is the issue for me. No approved agent targets the pathway, the STING credit is shared with Ishikawa, Vance and others, and I think recognition now would be early. I would revisit it in a few years once STING-directed drugs have shown clinical efficacy.

responses.point: El Manira also ranks B044 (TNF blockade) and the BCR-ABL and HPV vaccine candidates, and treats optogenetics (B014) as a methodological revolution that transformed circuit neuroscience, though six credited names exceed the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I share your view on B044, where Feldmann and Maini make a clean two-person configuration, and on the fact that B014 is a genuine revolution in method. My difficulty with optogenetics is the one you identify: six strong claimants cannot be honored with three, and any trio will look arbitrary to the field. I also give more weight to demonstrated human benefit. TNF blockade has two decades of clinical confirmation and is widely seen as the model for targeted cytokine therapy, which is why I hold it as my first alternative. I note that my own field is rheumatology, which gives me a perspective on B044 that I should state openly rather than present as neutral.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should be the third laureate, which depends on whether the committee wishes to honor identification of the active peptide or development of long-acting agonists, and whether Habener's absence from the credited names can be set aside.
The priority record for the active GLP-1 peptide, which I recall as disputed and cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether a two-part prize, for example GLP-1 together with a second distinct achievement, is feasible within the three-person cap, given that B041 alone already uses three names.
Whether the committee will treat the HPV (B010) and BCR-ABL (B009) candidates as overlapping with earlier prizes for HPV as a cause of cancer and for oncogene work.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My field is rheumatology and autoimmunity, which overlaps scientifically with B044 (TNF blockade) and, more distantly, with B029 (cGAS-STING), but shared subject matter is not a personal relationship, and I flag it for transparency only.
